nameStory: The Spiny Spider-flower gets its name from its distinctive flowers that look like long-legged spiders dancing on stems, with petals that seem to reach out like spider legs. The 'spiny' part comes from the small thorns or spines that dot the plant's stems, giving it a prickly personality to match its wild appearance.
description: Spiny Spider-flower is a tall, dramatic annual plant that can reach 3-6 feet in height with an upright, branching growth habit. Its most striking feature is clusters of unusual flowers with long, thin petals and extremely long stamens that extend far beyond the petals like spider legs. The plant has palmately compound leaves (shaped like an open hand) with 5-7 narrow leaflets, and the entire plant has a somewhat sticky, strong scent. As a tropical native that's been introduced to North America, it's quite rare in New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Distinctive spider-like flowers with 4 thin petals and extremely long stamens that extend 2-3 inches beyond the petals, creating a whisker-like appearance. Flowers are typically pink, purple, or white and arranged in dense clusters at stem tips.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Palmately compound leaves with 5-7 narrow, lance-shaped leaflets arranged like fingers on a hand. Leaves feel slightly sticky to the touch and have a strong, somewhat unpleasant odor when crushed.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall annual plant growing 3-6 feet high with an upright, branching structure. The whole plant has a somewhat weedy, wild appearance with multiple flowering stems.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Green stems dotted with small spines or thorns that you can feel when you run your hand along them. Stems are somewhat sticky and have the same strong scent as the leaves.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Long, narrow seed pods that stick out horizontally from the stem like thin fingers, eventually splitting open to release small seeds.

habitat: Extremely rare in New England, typically found as an escaped garden plant in disturbed areas, vacant lots, or near old homesteads where it may have been cultivated. Prefers full sun and well-drained soils, often appearing in weedy, disturbed ground rather than natural habitats.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring when soil warms. Young plants develop their characteristic palmate leaves and begin their rapid upward growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period from mid to late summer, when the spectacular spider-like flowers are most abundant and eye-catching. Plants reach full height during this season.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue into early fall, followed by the development of long seed pods. Plants begin to decline with first frost as they complete their annual cycle.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems and empty seed pods may persist through winter, but the plant is completely dormant as it's an annual that dies with frost.

funFact: This unusual flower is actually pollinated by bats in its native tropical habitat! The long stamens and nighttime fragrance are perfectly designed to dust pollen onto the furry faces of visiting bats as they hover and feed on nectar.
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with its close relative, the common Spider flower (Cleome houtteana), but Spiny Spider-flower has the distinctive small spines on its stems that you can actually feel, while common Spider flower is typically spineless or nearly so.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'spiny,' the thorns are actually quite small and more like tiny prickles - they won't seriously injure you but are definitely noticeable to the touch. This plant is sometimes grown in gardens for its unusual appearance but can self-seed and escape cultivation.
compareHints: Compared to the more common Spider flower (Cleome houtteana) found in gardens, Spiny Spider-flower is distinguished by its stem spines and generally more robust, wilder appearance. Both have the characteristic long-stamened spider-like flowers and palmate leaves, but only the spiny species has those telltale prickles along the stems that give it its name.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Spider flower is distinguished from its close relative spiny spider-flower (Cleome spinosa) by being generally taller and more robust in garden settings.
